subtopic: STATEMENT ON THREATENED RAILWAY STRIKE

speakeroldname: Hon. Milion F. Gregg (Minister of Labour):
subtopic: STATEMENT ON THREATENED RAILWAY STRIKE
speechtext:
In view of the importance of the matter, Mr. Speaker, may I make a brief statement to the house concerning the present railway dispute. Since the short statement I made a week ago today, hon. members will have seen reports in the press of the various meetings on the part of the negotiating committees in Montreal. They will have noted also from these reports that serious efforts were being made to find a solution to the problem. You will note that last night wires were sent to me from both groups of committees, outlining the discussions yesterday which indicated that some progress had been made but stating that they were not able to continue negotiations last night.
In acknowledging those wires this morning I decided that, rather than do so by sending a wire, I would telephone the leaders of the negotiating committees and ask them again if they could not find a solution by free collective bargaining. If I may be permitted, sir, I shall read to the house my summary, which I think is a fair one, of the message I conveyed, on the one hand to Mr. A. J. Kelly, who is associated with Mr. L. C. Malone on behalf of the men- Mr. Malone was near Mr. Kelly when I telephoned-and on the other hand to Mr. Donald Gordon, president of the Canadian National Railways, who was in consultation with Mr. W. A. Mather, president of the Canadian Pacific Railway, when I telephoned between 11 and 11.30 this morning. My summary is as follows:
Your wire of 27th January is acknowledged and I am making further reports on the whole matter to meeting of my colleagues this morning. In meantime a review of reports on your negotiations yesterday would indicate that a good
deal of progress was made in finding common grounds in respect to matters other than wages. Before asking cabinet to consider what attitude the government should take, as Minister of Labour, I would like to feel that every means for free and unhampered negotiations have been considered and reconsidered. Will the heads of your committees please confer by telephone or otherwise as soon as possible and I shall telephone by 2 p.m. today to learn results. I am anxious that full advantage be taken of the resources of unhampered collective bargaining.
I did telephone Mr. Gordon and Mr. Kelly at about two p.m., Mr. Speaker. They told me that a meeting had been arranged for three o'clock this afternoon. I indicated to them that I should like to get in touch with them before the house closes at six o'clock so that we might expect to have a report on any progress that might be made.

subtopic: BRIGADE TRAINING AREA
BRIGADE TRAINING AREA
speechtext:
1.	What sites were inspected in connection with the proposed brigade training area for Canadian troops?
2.	What are the names of the persons who made the inspections?
3.	Has a report been made in each case to the Department of National Defence?
4.	If so, will the report be made public?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
subtopic: BRIGADE TRAINING AREA
speechtext:
1.	With the expansion of the Canadian army, since the beginning of hostilities in Korea in June, 1950, and the contribution of the Canadian forces for the defence of western Europe under the North Atlantic treaty, it has become increasingly necessary to have an area in Canada large enough to permit the training in active service operations of a brigade and even larger formations. If possible, this area should be on the Atlantic seaboard so that it could be used for mobilization, final training and embarkation of formations that might be sent overseas to take their place in the forces of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization to prevent or stop aggression. Such an area should be located in a place where the climate permits training all the year round and where the ground has the characteristics that might be found in western Europe, with roads and other physical features permitting the employment of armoured and other vehicles and artillery and other weapons. Using existing information and also the results of new examinations, sites were looked

Ottawa, January 26, 1953 Memorandum to the Prime Minister:
Re Question No. 61 of Order Paper for January 26.
Mr. Knowles asks a series of questions with respect to the handling of copies and "any digest or summary" of the 1952 audit report to the House of Commons. The Minister of Finance is out of town today; therefore I address this memorandum to you.
The report is bound with volume I of the public accounts. Before the book was tabled on January 12, copies were delivered by the printing bureau to the Department of Finance, the audit office and, perhaps, to the joint parliamentary distribution branch. In addition the queen's printer distributes to the official mailing list and also stocks copies for sale. Consequently, a number of departments are involved.
Audit Office
The statutory direction is to make a report to the House of Commons. Consequently, all copies of the printed report which are delivered to the audit office are safekept by the assistant auditor general and myself until the Minister of Finance tables.
Annually, during the preparation of the report, numerous copies of the draft are in circulation throughout the audit office and, as a matter of established routine, supervisors of audit discuss some paragraphs with departmental and treasury officers in order to make certain that:
(a)	the text is factually correct; and
(b)	notice is being taken of all material facts.
I do not expect departments to concur in my views, but I endeavour to make certain that a fair statement of facts is given to the House of Commons. Paragraphs are brought to the notice of departments by use of clippings from either the draft text or printer's proofs. Whenever a supervisor thinks, after discussion, that a change in text should be considered, he discusses it with me and I decide.
Between August 25, 1952 (the date when I put a draft in circulation throughout the audit office) and October 27 (the date when the order to print was given) various paragraphs were brought to the notice of departmental and treasury officers. It was fortunate that we did so because, after the report was printed, a mistake was discovered by an officer of the Department of National Defence in paragraph 53 (page 23 of printed report). This paragraph deals with contributions to the services

pension account and stated that a total of $7,225,000 was in arrears. The national defence officer pointed out that the correct figure was $1,225,000, and this had the effect of making certain audit comment inaccurate and also some observations in paragraph 61 (page 25), which refers to the same subject. The queen's printer co-operated by reprinting four pages and pasting them in the already bound books. As a result, corrected figures and comment appear in the report as tabled and distributed.
No one likes to refer to his mistakes, but in this instance I'm particularly appreciative of the action of the national defence officer because some paragraphs in the report may be regarded as critical of national defence methods and it would have been easy, by keeping silent, "to put me over the barrel" by reference to the mistake after the report was tabled.

subtopic: SOUTH SASKATCHEWAN RIVER
SOUTH SASKATCHEWAN RIVER
speechtext:
1.	Did the Prime Minister, the Minister of Agriculture, or any other member or official of the government, either by letter, telegram or verbally, instruct officials of the P.F.R.A. not to appear before the royal commission on the South Saskatchewan river project?
2.	If so, for what reason?

subtopic: SOUTH SASKATCHEWAN RIVER
speechtext:
I have the answer here. It is as follows:
1 and 2. The royal commission on the South Saskatchewan river development was established to determine "whether the economic and social returns to the Canadian people on the investment in the proposed South Saskatchewan river project (central Saskatchewan development) would be commensurate with the cost thereof" and "whether the said project represents the most profitable and desirable use which can be made of the physical resources involved".
In pursuing their inquiry, the commissioners were afforded by their terms of reference, as is usual in references of this kind, such assistance and co-operation from all the departments of the government as they thought they might need. That they received such assistance from the P.F.R.A. throughout the whole of their inquiry is evident from the numerous acknowledgments contained in their report. Hon. members can refer, for instance, to pages 9, 43 and 45, where the commissioners make it clear that their task would have been impossible without the material and researches of the P.F.R.A. and the help of P.F.R.A. officials.
This commission was established to get information which the government did not already have and to make recommendations to it. As the commissioners had access to all the records and technical advice of the P.F.R.A., it was not necessary for them to have formal appearances by federal officials at public hearings. The government shared this view and gave this opinion to the officials of the P.F.R.A.
In reaching that conclusion, the government had in mind the fact that it would not be fair to place civil servants in a false position by requiring them to appear publicly and express opinions on matters on which the Minister of Agriculture and the government as a whole had subsequently to reach decisions.

speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability of investigating the economic condition of the fishing industry in Canada with a view to recommending legislation designed to render assistance to the industry comparable to the legislation already enacted to provide assistance for agriculture.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this resolution appeared on the order paper during the last session, but I did not have a chance to introduce it in the house during that time; consequently I took advantage of the fisheries estimates to go into the matter to some extent in June of last year. At that time in reply to the remarks I had made the then minister of fisheries (Mr. Mayhew) placed certain statements on Hansard which, in my opinion, did not in any way reply to the criticisms that I had placed before the house. I want to read a short portion of the remarks Mr. Mayhew made on June 19, 1952, as they appear at page 3435 of Hansard: This is what he had to say:
Well, I am not going to say that we are doing everything for the fishermen that we would like to do. I suppose the Minister of Agriculture would say the same about agriculture. But we should at least remember this. The total value of the fisheries to Canada last year, including Newfoundland, 
was $200 million. On the other hand, the total value of agriculture to Canada is $2 billion. There is a vast difference. If you compare the $10 million that we have-
That was the expenditure of the department. I continue:
-with the $60 million that agriculture has, you will see that it is not too far out of line ....
That statement would, in my opinion, indicate to the house that the Minister of Fisheries at that time was of the opinion that the assistance which was given agriculture was in no way much greater than the assistance which was given to the fishing industry. I explained that in my opinion there was a vast difference. I made a breakdown of the moneys that were voted for each department, which I mentioned on page 3426 of Hansard of that same day. As I say, I made a breakdown-perhaps estimated-of the moneys that were voted for the Department of Fisheries, and this is what I had to say:
The total vote for the fisheries department this year is nearly $10 million. If that figure is broken down it will be found that five-sixths of it or approximately $8,500,000 go to the employees of the department, leaving one-sixth, or $1,500,000, for other purposes connected with the industry; and five-sixths of this remainder, of $1,500,000 does not apply in any way to the province of New Brunswick. I refer to $700,000 for seal skins; $342,500 for bait service for Newfoundland; $240,000 for fisheries support board, Newfoundland, which leaves $160,000 for bounty payments for all the maritime provinces and $150,000 for the construction of drag-gers in all of the maritime provinces. With regard to the province of New Brunswick, my estimate would be that we would receive less than $100,000, including the bounty payments which, cost the taxpayers of this country not one single penny.
In reply to a question which I placed on the order paper some time ago with regard to loans under the farm loan board and the fisheries loan board for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1952, I received the following reply on June 4 from the Minister of Finance: Under the farm loan board, $4,238,400; under fisheries, $800. In other words, for every single dollar fishermen were granted, agriculture was given $5,298.

Then, assistance was given in connection with wheat it was not possible to harvest in the fall of 1951. Let me say to the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank), who has just interrupted, that I am not mentioning these things in any critical sense. I put the facts on record only so that hon. members may compare the assistance given to these two industries.
Fisheries
I am not making any criticism in respect to the assistance given in the Fraser valley or in any part of Canada. Indeed, I endorsed that assistance; I stood in the House of Commons and voted for it.
Then, assistance was given to the owners of cattle affected by the foot-and-mouth disease last year in Saskatchewan. We see that $20 million has been given to the apple growers of the Annapolis valley in Nova Scotia. I placed on record on the earlier occasion the fact that half a million dollars is given to the maple sugar producers of this country, by way of an annual grant.
I have read in the press recently an announcement that consideration is being given to a higher floor price for eggs. Again let me emphasize that I have not placed this list on record in any critical sense whatever. That assistance is being given, and it is beneficial to each and every one of us. I have voted that assistance of this kind should be given, and I would vote again to have it given, if I were called upon to do so.
I use these facts only for purposes of comparison, and to show, by the figures, that the fishermen of this country have received very little consideration, when compared with those who are engaged in agriculture. The only thing I ask is that they be considered in the same way.
Then, with regard to the problems which fishermen encounter from day to day in the province of New Brunswick, and particularly in my own county, I feel certain that a great percentage of those problems might be solved without the payment of a single dollar of subsidy, and without its costing this country one dollar.
Again in this connection I wish to quote from Hansard of June 19 where I explained the difficulties encountered by these fishermen in this day and age. Some of them are great problems, and mean the difference between keeping our young men at home, and in the industry, or having them go away to seek employment in other parts of Canada. That is the part that worries us most. We all like to keep our young men at home, in our own province or county.
On this earlier occasion, after I had set out some of the conditions, I said, as reported at page 3430 of Hansard of June 19, 1952:
I firmly believe that if anyone is prepared to criticize he should be in position at the same time to offer some constructive solution to the problem involved. For that reason I shall now suggest what in my opinion is the only course to follow in order to bring some semblance of stability to an industry which is now in a depressed condition and whose future is most gloomy indeed. In
1404

Fisheries
doing so I am confident that the course I shall suggest will be endorsed by every sardine fisherman in southern New Brunswick and in the state of Maine.
These sardine fishermen on both sides of the border must insist that the fisheries departments of the United States and Canada, together with the canners in both countries, get together immediately so that an opportunity will be provided for representatives of these fishermen to present their views and work out a plan whereby fishermen would be given a fair return for that which they produce. This has been accomplished in the past during the world wars and it was the only period in fifty years when fisherman and canner alike knew where they were going.
A stable price would benefit not only the fishermen, but the canners as well, and many canners I am sure will agree with that statement. A stabilized price would not cost the taxpayers of either country a single dollar.
During the periods I have mentioned, when prices were regulated by government action, no subsidies were paid by the government of either country. For example, the margin to the ultimate consumer as between sardines at $10 per hogshead and $20 per hogshead would be approximately 50 cents per case of 100 cans, or one-half cent per can. That differential would appear to be insignificant in so far as the consumer is concerned. It is a fundamental principle from the standpoint of the producer that this differential may mean the difference between stability and prosperity, on the one hand, and depression and chaos on the other.
That reminds me of a movement which has recently taken place in Saint John and Charlotte counties. These fishermen are attempting to form some kind of union. The movement has been in evidence during the last four weeks. They believe that collectively they will be in a better position to approach the Department of Fisheries and the government for some assistance in the way of floor prices in order to stabilize the industry. In my opinion that idea just will not work and I should like to explain why I have formed that opinion.
The particular section from which I come depends upon United States markets for the sale of two-thirds of what we produce. If we on the Canadian side of the border have a set price and try to compel United States canners to pay that price, they may resent that action being taken here. We have seen years when they were able to buy their total requirements from their own waters. Sardines are caught in the state of Maine just the same as in the counties of Charlotte and Saint John. If we had an established price the fishermen in the state of Maine would take full advantage of that. If there was a plentiful supply of sardines they would go to the Maine canners and say, "We are prepared to sell our sardines cheaper than the price set by the Canadian government." That would completely deny us our United States market.
For that reason I want to refer to the paragraph which I just quoted from the speech I

made last year, that the only way that this problem can ever be solved is internationally. Fishermen in the state of Maine are just as desirous as those in Canada that this action be taken. I want to impress upon the department and the government that this has been long delayed. I believe it is something that could be brought about without a great deal of trouble. The officials of the two fisheries departments could meet with the canning operators and discuss this problem and I believe firmly that the matter could be adjusted so that those who year after year have continued in this business without any stability whatever might know where they are going.
It is most discouraging to these producers to start up in the spring, put the last dollar they have back into the water and have to borrow some on which to go along to make preparations for another season, and then before those structures are completed to have the price of sardines drop by 50 per cent and in some cases a great deal more.
There is another problem facing the fishing industry to which I should like to refer, the cost of food servicing. It is quite apparent from my experience that those who have never produced a single ounce of wealth in this country expect unreasonable profits from that which is created by the sweat and labour of our primary producers. This applies to the agricultural as well as the fishing industries and to many other industries as well. I should like to refer to an article from the Lethbridge Herald which appeared in the Ottawa Journal of January 21, only a few days ago. This reads:
Egg Price Spread
Should it require 21 cents or 611 per cent to get a dozen grade A large eggs from the farmer producer to the city consumer? Egg prices have dropped lately and producers have been wondering. In Edmonton the producer gets 34 cents a dozen for grade A large, the wholesalers are charging 44 cents to retailers, and the retailers are charging 55 cents to consumers. We suppose if eggs dropped to 21 cents to consumers the producers would have to give them away in order that the costs of wholesaling and retailing might be paid. We're wondering if we're not going a little bit crazy in this matter of food servicing costs.
That is a matter that could be debated at some length. This problem is faced not only by the fishing industry but by the agricultural industry and many others. Only a few days ago I picked up a drug journal which indicated that the profits offered were nothing less than fabulous. Headlines guaranteed 42 per cent or 44 per cent profit on certain lines. The article I have just read indicates a 61 % per cent mark-up on a dozen eggs from the time it leaves the producer until it is in

the hands of the consumer. There is something wrong somewhere when it costs so much to merchandise an article.
I want to emphasize that those who reap that benefit in nine cases out of ten have never produced an ounce of wealth from the day they were born. But they are ready to take out every single bit of profit in order to crowd that farmer-producer down as far as it is possible to get him. I mentioned this same condition when I spoke last year and perhaps I should quote a short portion of my speech as reported at page 3432 of Hansard of June 19, 1952. After making several suggestions as to how assistance might be given to the fisheries, I then had this to say:
At the same time a full scale investigation into the spread between prices paid fishermen for groundfish such as cod, pollock and haddock and consumer prices might be in order. That might also apply to the prices consumers are obliged to pay in all parts of Canada for fish products. The great spread between the prices paid the producer and those paid by the consumer is something that should have been investigated long ago. The variation is too great between what the producer receives and the price that is being asked today of the consumers in this country. Such an investigation, I am sure, would bring to light a differential of most unfair proportions.
Two years ago fishermen in the county of Charlotte were catching pollock, one of the best fish we produce in Canada, and selling them for one-half cent per pound. The following winter I paid seventeen cents a pound for the finished article in my own home town. Many hon. members and many people may argue: If there is that great range of profit between the raw material and the finished article, why is it more fishermen do not finish the article themselves? I can say without any thought of contradiction that the great majority of these fishermen have not facilities for taking care of the fish. It means quite an investment in fish sheds, hogsheads, tons of salt and all that goes with it. In a great many cases you would have to wait at least three, four or five months before you received a single dollar because it would take that length of time. By the time the fish are split, salted and ready for sale three, four or five months have passed. It is utterly impossible for fishermen to go that length of time without any recompense. Again I want to make the point that in nine cases out of ten where I have asked for assistance to build fish houses by way of loans, in order that the fishermen might do the very thing I have described, the requests have been turned down completely. Year after year I have tried to have some provision made whereby fishermen could be given assistance 68108-901
Fisheries
in cases such as I have outlined, and in nine cases out of ten such requests have been ignored.
I might also add that as a rule it is the little fellow who has been turned down. If any assistance was given it was extended to those who perhaps might have been able to get by without it; but those who actually needed it, those who were producing, were the ones who did not receive the assistance to which I believe they are entitled. There are many fishing villages down there where after a bad storm the fishermen have lost their fish houses and every bit of gear they had by which to make a livelihood. When the storm was over it was all gone. Perhaps the boat was gone too. But there is no provision whereby I can come to the government and get any assistance. It is just not granted. If they go to a bank for money and have no security it is utterly impossible to get assistance there. That is the position in which they are placed. I want hon. members to compare that situation with what has happened when terrible things have occurred in the field of agriculture. In every case- and I support it 100 per cent-assistance has been given. A way has been found to get the farmers out of their trouble.
I am glad that a way has been found. I do not mean to be critical in any sense of the word, but I do feel that discrimination should not be shown. Look at what has been done for the gold mining industry. I have supported such action and have never criticized it. In every other industry where primary producers have been involved, with the exception of fishing, a way has been found to help them out of their difficulties. The fishing industry, however, has been ignored over the years. I have every hope that conditions may improve and that we will consider that fishermen should be treated in the same way as other primary producers.
I should like to refer briefly again to fishermen's insurance and to quote briefly from page 3427 of Hansard of June 19, 1952, when the estimates of the Department of Fisheries were before us and I spoke on this matter. On that occasion I said:
During this session we have heard many suggestions with regard to some type of insurance to protect all types of fishing equipment. Before I get too far away from my main subject, I should like to suggest a way in which an insurance plan might be established, which would give the fishermen some protection, and at the same time the fishermen themselves would be contributing. In no way would this place any financial burden on the taxpayers of this country. I refer to the $160,000 which is paid in bounties and distributed among thousands of fishermen each year in payments ranging from $5 to $10, regulated of course by the number eligible for payment and by the number of applications received. This bounty is of little assistance to the industry, and although H

Fisheries
am not familiar with insurance rates I am convinced that $160,000 would pay the premium on an enormous amount of insurance and give those fishermen a protection which is considered very necessary in other industries but has never applied to the great part of the fisherman's property used in his hazardous calling.
It might be necessary for the government to supplement this payment by some amount, but I suggest it to the department for their consideration, and also to get the reaction from the fishermen themselves. I believe it would be a move in the right direction, and would be endorsed by the majority of the fishermen in the maritime provinces.
After I made that statement the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) spoke on the subject at some length and endorsed the statement I had made. Then the Hon. Mr. Mayhew, who was then minister of fisheries, replied, and his remarks can be found at page 3435 of Hansard of June 19, 1952. He had this to say:
The hon. member for Charlotte brought out the idea-and it was referred to by the hon. member for Cape Breton South-that the $160,000 that is paid as a bounty should be used for insurance purposes. In the hon. member's own riding there are 146 boat owners and 181 fishermen working on the boats, or a total of 327 men, in the county of Charlotte who are getting some of this money. In the whole of the maritime provinces there are 14.358 men. It would be very difficult to get all of these men to agree to cancel their right, which amounts to a little more than $6 apiece; it amounts to $9.55 each. That is what it amounted to last year.
The hon. member for Cape Breton South said that it was a variable amount. It is not exactly a variable amount; it is the interest on $4 million. That is the amount on which the interest is based. I think it would be difficult to get an agreement from the 14,358 fishermen that their money should be used to pay for insurance-
It would be very interesting to know whether, at the time the arrangement was made for bounty, payments to fishermen, all the 14,000, if there were that many at that time in the maritime provinces, were interviewed collectively or otherwise to secure their permission to use this money for that purpose. From the minister's statement it would seem that it would be utterly impossible at the present time to use the money for any other purpose without the permission of the 14,000 fishermen in the maritime provinces. The amount is on the record for the little county of Charlotte from which I come, and in the particular year referred to by the then minister of fisheries the fishermen of that county received about $3,000. That sum would not pay for one small boat if it were lost tomorrow. Surely there must be some way that members of the House of Commons can amend the regulation so that the money can be used for insurance rather than for the purpose to which it is being put at the present time.

I agree that if the majority of the fishermen were opposed to the idea I would not support it myself. I offer it as a suggestion. It seems absurd to me to think for one minute that in order to amend the regulation each individual fisherman in the maritime provinces will have to be consulted. I believe that is the job of members of parliament and I believe we have every right to do so if we wish.
The men who follow this hazardous calling are proud, independent citizens seeking a livelihood from the harvests of the sea. They do not ask for nor accept assistance from any source if conditions are such that a fair return may result from their long hours of toil. Owing to the lack of organization, which has been attempted on many occasions without success, and the complete failure of the old law of supply and demand to solve the problem, I most sincerely appeal to the Department of Fisheries and the government to regard the problems of these rugged individuals in the same light and with the same sympathetic consideration and understanding that has been accorded other primary producers in Canada. Let us as Canadians make every effort to have these fishermen included within that group whose standard of living has been so greatly improved by the guidance and assistance of this federal organization.

subtopic: SUGGESTED INVESTIGATION OF ECONOMIC CONDITIONS IN FISHING INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I could not allow this opportunity to pass without rising to reassert my entire support of the fishermen of the maritime provinces and particularly of my native county of Gloucester. I wish to congratulate my colleague, the hon. member for Charlotte (Mr. Stuart), on presenting this resolution to this house, and I must tell him at the outset that I am entirely in accord with it. It pleases me a great deal to be once in a while on the same side as the hon. member for Charlotte.
This resolution, Mr. Speaker, is of particular interest to my constituents and to me, for several reasons. First, it is of interest because of the importance of the fishing industry in our economy; second, because of the great losses suffered by the fishermen throughout the years in gear, vessels and men. Finally, it is of interest because this resolution is patterned, at least in its broader lines, on certain remarks and suggestions which I made in my maiden speech in this house on June 19 last, which remarks I repeated in my speech of December, 1952. I have always championed the cause of the fishermen. As I said in my maiden speech, I am a descendant of French Acadian fishermen, and I am proud of my

Fisheries
ancestry. I have always classified the fishing industry as one of the most important, if not the most important, in my native county of Gloucester.
In view of the new gigantic mining development in the vicinity of my town of Bathurst in the county of Gloucester, just lately come to light, I feel that in the very near future I may be able to stand in this house and mention the new Gloucester zinc, lead, copper and silver mines, not only as the most important industry in my constituency and my province of New Brunswick but as the biggest discovery in its line in the whole history of Canadian mining. Nevertheless, the fishing industry will continue to be a most vital cog in the economic gears of my county and province. I fully agree with the following paragraph in the last bulletin of the fisheries council of Canada, and I quote:
Unlike most of our basic resources, our fisheries of sea, lake and stream are self-renewing, and will provide work, wealth and food in perpetuity if carefully managed and protected.
I have stated the main reason for my support of this resolution, and that is because of the importance of the industry in my constituency.
At this stage, may I be permitted to digress from my main thought by saying that when I came to this house last June I had a great preconceived admiration for the western members of this house, and I still entertain that same admiration. Why? Because, Mr. Speaker, long before coming into this house, through reading Hansard and by following the newspapers, I found that the western members, be they Conservative, Liberal, C.C.F. or Social Crediters, whenever there was a question of interest to the agricultural industry in the west, always jumped in the same dory and rowed together until they made port. I congratulate them on so doing. Although I am a young member here and a novice and perhaps should not make any suggestion, yet may I be permitted to suggest to the hon. members from the maritime provinces, notwithstanding their political affiliations-and I appeal also to the members from the Pacific coast without any reservation as to political affiliation-that they join together in presenting a united front so that eventually we may be able to obtain from this house some of the things the member for Charlotte has suggested. I repeat what I have said before, that the fishermen of the maritime provinces particularly are the forgotten children, the orphans in the family of Canadian confederation.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I have underlined the importance of the fishing industry in my constituency. I shall not repeat what I have
said before along those lines. May I, however, quote from the best available information as to the value of our fleet. We have a fleet of new dragger type vessels operating from the county of Gloucester consisting of 31 class 50 feet and class 60 feet vessels, at an aggregate value of $682,000 and with a total complement of 133 sailors. We have also about 850 motorized and sail schooners and smaller boats, of an aggregate value of $212,000 with a total complement of 1,700 sailors. Hence, we have vessels to the value of almost $1 million, with a complement of 1,833 men employed as sailors or fishermen, operating from my county. This figure does not take into account the thousands and thousands of dollars invested by our fishermen in lobster traps, in our famous oyster fishery, in our nets for herring, salmon or mackerel; nor does the figure of 1,833 men employed as sailors take account of our young men employed in fishing our famous oyster farms and beds, in clam digging, or the hundreds of men and women employed in our fish processing plants such as our lobster canneries, our clam canneries and our freezers. These figures, and the addition I have made to them by referring to the rest of our fishing population, will give this house some idea of the importance of the industry to my county.
Passing now to a subject which has been touched upon by the member for Charlotte, I should like to mention the losses sustained by the fishermen of Gloucester county. I have mentioned this subject to the house whenever the opportunity arose. I am very pleased, Mr. Speaker, that the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair) is in the house. I am pleased to say to this house that I have had nothing but co-operation from the minister and his department in the probably all too numerous demands I have addressed to him. It is impossible to give a complete picture of the losses sustained by our fishermen throughout the years. There were no statistics kept 25 or 30 years ago, whereas our fish inspectors and fish supervisors in my county are doing a good job in keeping track of everything now. I believe that we have now the best available information so far as all branches of our fisheries are concerned.
May I also say-and this may be of interest to the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair) -that conditions have changed over the years. In former years, Mr. Speaker, all or practically all of our vessels, schooners and fishing boats, were owned by companies- such as Robin, Jones and Whitman or such as the Loggie companies-and the schooners and fishing boats were rented to our fishermen, fully equipped. They were rented to our fishermen for a certain annual rent or

Fisheries
consideration. Hence the companies were assuming all risk of loss. When there was a broken cable, a torn sail or even when there was a total loss, the whole thing was absorbed by the owners or the companies. But there has been a marked evolution in fisheries in our county.
Through the help of these co-operatives and, through strict economy on the part of our captains and of our sailors, I think I can safely say that today our fishermen own most if not all of the vessels and fishing gear in my county. We are now faced with the situation that when we have a loss, either minor or major, the captain or the ship owner must bear the loss. Someone may say: Why not carry insurance on those ships against marine risk and against fire risk? My reply would be that if you would just take the trouble to consult the table of standard rates of insurance on those ships, you would immediately conclude that our fishermen simply do not have the means to do so.
May I refer to some of the major losses in the Gloucester county fishing fleet since the turn of the century. In 1900 we had, in the gulf of St. Lawrence, this awful storm which caused the Gloucester county fishing fleet the loss of nine fishing schooners and of thirty-five fishermen who were drowned at sea. In 1914-the year of the outbreak of the first war-there was another terrific storm in the gulf; and again our Gloucester county fleet was penalized by the loss of six big schooners and twenty-two fishermen who lost their lives on that occasion. Of course in those days no claim was ever filed for loss because, I suppose, nobody knew how to do it. In any event, no claims were filed and consequently nothing was ever paid to these fishermen.
In 1921, Mr. Speaker, an incident occurred whilst I was attending college and during the summer holidays while I was myself on a schooner owned and captained by one of my late uncles. While we were attempting to make Shippigan gully during the height of a storm in June, I personally witnessed a spectacle which I shall never forget; I cannot forget it. At the very entrance of Shippigan gully, at the bar-that is the sand bar but it is called "the bar" in fishermen's language -I saw a St. Simon schooner hit the bar and break in two with the resulting loss of the lives of Captain Doiron and his crew of four.
Now that the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier) is in the house I make to him a special appeal for the necessary credits so that the famous Shippigan gully will be properly dredged at the earliest possible opportunity. If the Minister of Public

Works will only consult with the officials of his department, he will find that this important entrance in the northern part of the province-it is really the funnel or the link between the gulf and Chaleur bay-has not been touched by a dredge for at least thirty years.

subtopic: SUGGESTED INVESTIGATION OF ECONOMIC CONDITIONS IN FISHING INDUSTRY
speechtext: Shame.

subtopic: SUGGESTED INVESTIGATION OF ECONOMIC CONDITIONS IN FISHING INDUSTRY
speechtext:
During the Christmas recess several captains of draggers were at my office and they said to me: Robichaud, you must come with me next summer-and I will-out of Shippigan in order to see for yourself the pitiful conditions with which we are faced. Some of these draggers-in fact most of them-oftentimes have to come in from a distance of eighty to ninety miles at sea, in the dark, during the thick of a storm and enter Shippigan gully, which is a narrow one. You may not appreciate as I do the danger with which such trips are fraught; but I am making to the Minister of Public Works a special appeal that this Shippigan gully matter be fully investigated and that the necessary dredging be done at once so that we shall not have any more casualties amongst our fishing fleet.
In the years 1949, 1950, 1951 and 1952, according to the best available information, I am told that our total losses in fishing gear, nets, lobster traps and so on amounted to $24,800. Last year our bay inshore fishermen suffered extensive damage to their fishing gear. This matter has been brought to the attention of the Department of Fisheries and I must thank the Minister of Fisheries for the ruling which has recently been made. I wish to refer to the damage caused by the dragging operations of our draggers in Chaleur bay to the fishing apparatus and gear owned by the inshore fishermen. Last year and the year before, Mr. Speaker, our inshore fishermen lost thousands and thousands of dollars in gear which was swept away when draggers came too near to shore and dragged everything away, including nets, trawls and lobster traps. In all fairness and justice it seems to me there should be some way or means of remunerating these inshore fishermen for these losses. They lay their trawls, set their nets, set their lobster traps, mark them with buoys and a post which is six or seven feet above water; and these draggers come along, drag all along the coast and carry everything away. Is this encouragement to these hardy toilers of the sea, our inshore fishermen?
At the end of December, 1952, or the beginning of January 1953, there was a big fire at the Blanchard machine shop in Le Bou-thillier P.O., in the parish of Caraquet. This

machine shop is the only place to which our dragger captains and owners could bring their motors or the parts of their motors or dragging gear to be repaired during the lay-off in the winter season. I have here a list of losses sustained by our dragger owners and captains on account of that fire and amounting to over $20,000. The lowest figure on this list is $150 and they go as high, for one dragger captain, as $4,000, which means that he lost his diesel motor completely. Again it may be said: Why do the captains not insure against fire? Again I repeat-and I know whereof I speak-that our captains simply cannot afford to pay the standard rates of fire insurance against their boats, vessels and gear.
I should like to cite another concrete and specific instance of loss which our fishermen sustained and for which they were never compensated. Some two years ago, during the height of a storm in Chaleur bay a big boom of pulpwood was broken by the storm. Hundreds and hundreds of cords of pulpwood came ashore. The nets of our salmon fishermen in Petit Rocher, Beresford and Nigadoo suffered damages amounting to thousands and thousands of dollars. Their claims were submitted to the pulp mill companies who owned the pulpwood, but of course they put up their hands and pleaded that it was an act of God and that was the end of it.
I submit that facts like these, matters like these, damages such as I have related to this house, which are not the result of my imagination, but concrete, specific cases which have occurred in my own county, should be considered by the Department of Fisheries whenever any agency is set up such as has been suggested by the hon. member for Charlotte.
Hon. gentlemen will recall that last year I rose in my place in this house as a green member-I am still quite green, but not as green as I was then-and I put a question to the then minister of fisheries, the Hon. Mr. Mayhew, and asked him whether any claims had been filed, or whether there was any possibility of our fishermen getting any remuneration for the losses they had suffered through storms. Reference to Hansard will reveal that the answer given to me by the then minister of fisheries was to the effect that no claims had been filed. I now bring to your attention, Mr. Speaker, and particularly to the attention of the Minister of Fisheries, a particular instance of a claim, and a big one, which was filed in due form in 1950. Of course that was before the present Minister of Fisheries occupied his position.
Fisheries
It was filed by the fishermen of Northumberland county, which is our neighbouring county. I am sorry that the hon. member representing Northumberland, N.B. (Mr, Mc-William) is not in his seat today, because I feel sure he would corroborate what I am about to say. The total losses suffered by the smelt fishermen of the county of Northumberland during December, 1949, and January, 1950, amounted to the gigantic sum of $81,256. This was substantiated in toto, Mr. Speaker, by a detailed statement of fifteen pages containing the names and addresses of all the fishermen who had suffered damage; the number of nets, the size of nets, the number of leaders lost and the total of each individual claim were submitted to the Department of Fisheries in the summer of 1950. A suggestion was also made at that time by the central committee of the Northumberland county fishermen that a special commission should be set up by the Department of Fisheries consisting of a chairman appointed by the federal government, with representation on the commission from the Department of Fisheries, and one member to be appointed by the fishermen themselves.
The purpose of the proposed commission was to inquire into the then existing conditions of the fishing industry of the neighbouring county of Northumberland. It was also further suggested that one of the commission's first duties would be to inquire into and decide whether the enormous losses suffered by the Northumberland county smelt fishermen during the season just past were the normal hazards of the trade, or whether they might be considered in the nature of an act of God. My information is that the proposed commission was never set up; nor were the Northumberland smelt fishermen ever compensated for their great losses of smelt fishing equipment in December 1949 and January 1950.
The attitude-and this is what I want to bring to the attention of the house-the attitude of the Department of Fisheries at that time was one of the so common pass-the-buck attitudes which I have had occasion to observe on the part of the government during the few short months that I have been here. The decision rendered in the late summer of 1950 by the Department of Fisheries was to the effect that whilst the losses were unquestionably serious to the fishermen, the said losses-and mark these words-the said losses do not appear to have reached the extent which could be classified as a calamity of national significance, and that any compensation which might be paid would fall into the category of relief which, generally speaking,

Fisheries
according to the ruling we received from the Department of Fisheries, was purely a provincial responsibility.
I was very much surprised to see that word "relief" in the departmental ruling, because I thought that this government looked upon the word "relief" with holy horror. But what astounds me, Mr. Speaker, is that no consideration is given by the departmental authorities to claims submitted for losses by fishermen unless and until they reach the stage of a calamity of national significance.
As the hon. member for Charlotte (Mr. Stuart) has suggested, why should we not be put on a par with the western farmers? He has voted in favour of assistance to the western farmers, and if I have the opportunity to vote to assist the western farmer I shall do so. But we are simply asking this house to give our fishermen fair, just and equitable treatment, and not make fish of one and flesh of another.
May I now deal with the question of more recent losses. I am glad that my colleague, the hon. member for Kent, N.B. (Mr. Leger), is in his seat. May I refer to the Evangeline, our French newspaper of Moncton, N.B., of January 20. I find an article relating to the losses of the smelt fishermen of Buctouche in the county of my hon. friend. According to this article the smelt fishermen of Buctouche bay have lost more than 60 nets carried away by the ice through Northumberland strait. The minimum loss, according to the article in the newspaper, is set at $6,000, with a possibility of reaching a maximum of $10,000. These figures, Mr. Speaker, are in addition to the losses of the catch before the nets can be replaced.
I have attempted to give concrete evidence, specific instances, of losses suffered by our fishermen by storms and moving ice. Ice does not give any advance notice before it moves. These losses have been suffered by our fishermen not only of the county of Gloucester, but in the neighbouring county of Northumberland and some in the sister county of Kent.
I now come to the resolution itself. My analysis of this resolution, which I heartily support, reveals that its object is to obtain legislation to render to the fishing industry assistance comparable to the legislation already enacted in favour of agriculture, and to attain this end some investigation must be carried out, as the resolution suggests, and it ought to be conducted into the economic conditions of our fishing industry. In my opinion the investigation mentioned in the resolution should not be carried out by a commission or
[Mr. Robichaud.l
a fact-finding board or a board of inquiry, call it what you may, composed solely of departmental employees.
I have nothing but the greatest respect and admiration for the biologists and the technologists of the Department of Fisheries. They really have performed, in the field of fishing, feats which border on the miraculous. As concrete evidence of my assertion may I refer to an article in the same French newspaper of New Brunswick, the Evangeline. I do not know whether any of the hon. gentlemen have read this article. I find in this French newspaper of New Brunswick, in its issue of January 20, 1953, an article which deals with the treatment of trout with aureomycin. This article reveals that recently the piscicultural establishment at Jasper national park has produced a more vigorous trout by adding to its ordinary food this magic drug known as aureomycin. It is reported that during thirteen weeks in the Jasper national park fish hatchery small quantities of aureomycin were given to some 3,000 small, young trout. After that period of time the young trout which had been thus treated were, on the average-and this is very interesting-a quarter of an inch longer than those which had been provided only with their customary ration. Moreover, according to the article, the normal death or loss rate among the latter group was three times greater than among the young trout whose food had been treated with small doses of aureomycin. This is one more instance of the miraculous feats performed in the study of fish by biologists and technologists in the Department of Fisheries.
In my submission, however, in order to conduct a thorough and practical investigation into the economic difficulties of the fishing industry of Canada, the Department of Fisheries would be well advised to have representatives of fish dealers and some practical and experienced fishermen serving on a board of inquiry or commission, to work alongside departmental experts. Great care should also be exercised in order that every important branch of the fishing industry in Canada may be represented, and properly represented, on such a fact-finding body. I contend that the cod fishermen or the salmon fishermen can give no practical assistance to the sardine fishermen, and vice versa.
Granted, therefore, that every important branch of the industry be properly represented, with due regard to the particular problems attendant upon each major producing area in our dominion, I feel we would at last have a real, practical and sensible board of inquiry or investigation.

On such a board, experts in biology and technology would have the opportunity to marry their knowledge with the practical experience and common-sense suggestions offered by men in the trade. Under these conditions I believe the Canadian fishing industry could naturally and logically expect great results.
Commissions composed of so-called experts and technicians, however high and numerous their qualifications may have been, have been touring Canada and will no doubt continue to do so at great expense to the Canadian taxpayer, and have always reminded me-and this long before I came to this House of Commons-of a famous saying of one of our French fabulists: "La montagne qui enfante une souris." When stated in English this means: "A mountain brings forth a mouse." I suggest therefore to the Department of Fisheries that should it give favourable consideration to this resolution-and I hope it will-it should bear in mind that the fishermen of Canada will expect concrete results and not mere empty propositions; practical effectiveness rather than theoretical deductions in the study of their problems. Perhaps when I say this I should confine my observations to the fishermen of Gloucester, and I shall do so. They will not accept any vague proposition.
The fishermen have many problems. In order to reach this goal the Department of Fisheries should therefore make a special effort to democratize any board of inquiry or commission it may consider setting up. By bringing such board or commission closer to the fishermen of Canada it would assure a report which would be really beneficial to the fishing industry throughout the country.
In order to be logical, after having offered certain suggestions perhaps I should go further-dealing always with the resolution- and amplify some of the nice points my good friend from Charlotte (Mr. Stuart) has underlined. What are the remedies for the pitiful situation of the fishermen about whom my hon. friend has spoken-as a matter of fact, the fishermen of Canada?
There may be many remedies, but I have a few I should like to suggest to the house and bring to the attention particularly of the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair) and his department. In my maiden speech in the House of Commons on June 19, 1952, I said:
I therefore feel justified in asking the Minister of Fisheries to give immediate attention to the matter, with a view to setting up,-and this is the important point-a system of federal aid to compensate our fishermen for the heavy losses they sustain through storms.
Fisheries
Since there is no hesitation in granting aid to farmers and stock-breeders during epidemics, why not give assistance to the fishermen who are constantly victims of the worst plague there is- and I know something about it-storms at sea.
Again, speaking in the house on December 1 last I made this suggestion, as it is reported at pages 230 and 231 of Hansard:
Before concluding my remarks on the question of fisheries, may I again stress the necessity of providing fishermen with some form of remuneration for losses sustained through storms. I am informed that a plan is now under advisement by the Department of Fisheries to establish a permanent program of insurance as well as loans-interest free, I hope-to storm-stricken fishermen. May I advocate the elaboration of a system following the broad outline of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act which has proved to be highly beneficial to western farmers. I am also in favour of extending the plan now under study so as to embrace some kind of cheap contributory insurance not alone on the fishing equipment but on the lives of our fishermen as well. After all, there is in my submission no more hazardous occupation than that of those hardy and courageous toilers of the sea who risk everything and face the ever-recurring dangers of storm and sea in order to develop the fishing grounds of Canada's Atlantic and Pacific coasts, which are recognized as the richest in the world. Hence special consideration should be given by our government to the welfare of Canada's fishermen; and a protective scheme of assistance and insurance is indeed long past due.
May I now refer to a system of social security which, I am told, has been in vogue in France for a number of years, a system I would advise the Department of Fisheries to study with great care. This system of social security in France is concerned not only with fishermen but also covers the young men in the merchant marine of that country.
After I had spoken in the house in June of last year a friend of mine, Mr. H. M. Rive from Caraquet, N.B., a man who, because of having been brought up in the fishing industry, is an expert in fisheries questions, a man who has specialized in that industry during his lifetime, wrote an article in our weekly paper in Gloucester, the Gloucester Northern Light in which he referred to the system in France which affords social security to the fishermen and merchant marine of that country. This article dated July 7, 1952, states-

Thank you.
Referring to this system of social security in France the article states:
The first condition is that the prospective candidate for either career must have attended school until the age of 13. On applying, his name is

Fisheries
entered in a register opposite a number, which will ensure his identity for life, after he has served a month's apprenticeship.
At the age of 50, he is entitled to an annual pension, provided he has fished or followed the sea for 300 months. At his death, his wife continues to receive half the pension, and the children under 16, an allowance of so much a day, as long as the mother remains a widow.
Provision is made also for what is called proportional indemnity in case of death before 50, and for a provident indemnity in cases of sickness or injury, while engaged in his particular work. His personal belongings, also, are insured against loss by fire, shipwreck or any other cause, incidental to his occupation.
I hope the Department of Fisheries will study this scheme of social security for fishermen which has been in force for a number of years in France and which I am told is working very well.
Before resuming my seat I should like to direct attention to a recent threat to our famous lobster industry. A British United Press dispatch to Evangeline, our daily French newspaper published in Moncton, New Brunswick, states that a bill is to be introduced very soon in the Massachusetts state legislature to compel exporters of fresh lobster meat to pasteurize their product rather than to preserve it by refrigeration as has heretofore been the practice. I submit to the Department of Fisheries that most of our fresh lobster meat exporters will have to go out of business if that bill goes through.
This article of January 21 states that this same bill provides for the exclusion of Canadian fresh and frozen lobster from the Boston market, which is the most profitable market we have. I have a question on the order paper about this, but I am bringing this up at this time as I believe it is of urgent importance. I ask the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair) to tell the house what steps have been taken to block this measure.
A similar bill was presented some years ago in the same state legislature. The fishermen of the maritime provinces organized themselves without any help from Ottawa. They hired a lawyer in Boston and the bill was blocked, but we cannot be hiring Boston lawyers every day. I think this is a matter for the attention of the federal government.
I thank the house for letting me have a few minutes extra. I am heartily in accord with the resolution submitted by the hon. member for Charlotte (Mr. Stuart). I hope the principles that we have underlined and the concrete suggestions which we have submitted to the Department of Fisheries will receive favourable attention. I know the Minister of Fisheries has the development, the expansion and the future of the industry at heart.

Mr. Speaker, I support the resolution moved by the hon. member for Charlotte (Mr. Stuart). I am sorry that my deskmate, the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis), is not here because he is a member of the fisheries committee and has always been most prominent in taking up cudgels on behalf of the fishermen. I congratulate the hon. member for Charlotte upon bringing forward this resolution, which reads:
That, in the opinion of the house, the government should consider the advisability of investigating the economic condition of the fishing industry in Canada with a view to recommending legislation designed to render assistance to the industry comparable to the legislation already enacted to provide assistance for agriculture.
I want to assure the hon. member and other fishermen in the house that I am in favour of their getting as much assistance as agriculture gets. I do not think it should be only one way. This investigation would not be ahead of time because I know of many fishermen who are going broke today. The two previous members who spoke are fishermen, and I have not their experience. I have gone out on the herring fishing boats on the river Clyde as a boy, and I have been out on the lakes of Manitoba once or twice, but that does not justify me in saying that I am a fisherman.
I wonder if the hon. member who introduced this resolution intended it to apply to the prairie fisheries. As the hon. gentleman knows, fishing on the prairies is under the provincial governments but the problems there are the same. When the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair) speaks in the debate I hope he will clear up that point. I should like to see the prairie fisheries included in the investigation suggested by the hon. member.
There may be some hon. members who have never been west and who may be interested in knowing that in Manitoba we have lakes over 400 miles long, where the storms are bigger than any I have seen on the Atlantic. The fishermen out there are facing difficult times. They are getting a very low price for their fish, and I think it only right and proper that some form of floor or guaranteed price be provided as is done in the case of agricultural products, so they may obtain a fair return for the services they render.
Someone may say that if a floor price is set there will be too many fishermen. That cannot take place on the lakes in Manitoba because the catch is regulated; there can be only so many fish caught each year. During the war we had a guaranteed and set price and the fishermen got a square deal, the

processors got a square deal and the consumers got a square deal. I do not think there would be any harm in bringing something like that back again.
I think the fishermen could help themselves a great deal by co-operative methods. I have suggested to former ministers of fisheries that in the grant made for co-operative education something should be provided for the co-operative education of the fishermen of the prairie provinces. Up to the present time I have never been able to get anything for Manitoba or the other two prairie provinces.
The new Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair) is progressive, and a go-ahead type. I will not praise him * any more because, knowing his past history, I do not think it would agree with him. However, I hope that one of these days he will give some consideration to seeing that we get a few dollars out of what is set aside for co-operative education.
I do not want to take up a lot of time. I support the motion, and if anything is done I want it to apply to prairie fishing. I should like to see guaranteed prices. As I have already said, the catch is regulated so that there would not be too many fish caught, or too many people getting rich quickly.
We have terrific storms on lake Winnipeg and lake Manitoba. The fishermen there also lose their boats and gear and run into all kinds of difficulty. We subsidize people who dig for gold. I think people who produce food are more entitled to assistance than people who dig for gold. I want to endorse the resolution again, and when the minister replies I hope he will tell me whether the resolution can apply to prairie conditions.

speechtext:
I, too, should like to join the other members, Mr. Speaker, in offering my congratulations to the hon. member for Charlotte (Mr. Stuart). It is gratifying to see that this session we have had two afternoons devoted to a debate on fisheries, whereas normally we just get one day to discuss the affairs of perhaps the most important department of government. It is certainly the most important department to those of us who live in the maritime provinces. We have a great many debates on agriculture around this house, but very few on fisheries. I sometimes think that perhaps the same consideration is not given to fisheries that is given to agriculture by members of the cabinet. I should like to point out to the members of the cabinet that the Lord was fairer. They will recall the miracle of the loaves and fishes, and I am quite sure they will recall that He treated the loaves and fishes in the same way. Perhaps that is a good thought for the cabinet to keep in the back of their minds.
Fishermen are very independent people, and I believe we are quite proud of that fact. Perhaps they have been too independent in the past. It seems to me that they do not realize the truth of the old adage that the squeaking wheel gets the grease. Certainly since I came down here in 1945 I have heard a great many squeaks from members representing agricultural ridings, and perhaps not enough from those representing the fishermen.
Now we have a new Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair). I have the greatest confidence in him, and believe he will bring a new approach to this problem. I might just point out to him

I do not know whether or not there is anything indicative about this

that both he and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) are fortunate enough to have been named "Jimmy". Whether or not there is any connotation to that word that might have something to do with prying money loose from the treasury board, I hope he works it to the greatest possible extent.
At one time you and I, Mr. Speaker, had the good fortune to visit a prairie town in company with our good friend the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Thatcher). There was not as much activity in that town as there is in the average fishing town. Fishermen always seem to have to rush around in order to make a living. On the occasion

Fisheries
when we went to this prairie town, it reminded us of Goldsmith's deserted village. We ran into our good guide and mentor who said, "I know where the boys will be; they will be down at the curling rink." We went down there because it was the only place in town completely surrounded by expensive automobiles. We went in there and met some charming people, friends of his, and also some Liberals, I think. There was a furious argument going on as to the relative merits of Cadillacs, Buicks and Chrysler Imperials, and whether they were good for hunting ducks or touring Mexico. I said to the hon. member for Moose Jaw, "Where is your statue?" He said, "There was no war around here to which we have to raise a statue." I said, "No, but surely you must have a statue of the Minister of Agriculture; surely these people would not be so unappreciative that they would not have a statue of him." He said, "No, they have not." I can tell the Minister of Fisheries that if he does one quarter as much for the fishermen as the Minister of Agriculture has done for the farmers, he will live forever in bronze in every small fishing village.
Let us take a look at pork, for instance. We got into a little trouble in the pork business a short time ago because of the United States embargo. This cabinet acted with furious speed, I thought with almost unseemly haste. They acted, first of all, to ensure that the producer of pork got a profit. That was fine, and I was glad to hear it. They made sure that the packer who canned that pork got a profit. Then the government turned around and sold that pork to the Canadian consumer at less than cost. Well, perhaps one could argue that was a virtuous thing for them to do.
What happened when the salmon canners got into the same position? We were cut out of the United Kingdom market by a virtual embargo because of the United Kingdom's lack of dollars. The government did not step in in any way to try to stabilize that market and to prevent the distress selling that actually took place. As a result one of our largest fishery co-operatives in British Columbia went bankrupt. That was an unfortunate circumstance for a large number of fishermen there. I may say that every large fishing company in British Columbia lost large sums of money this past year. After all, when a company out there loses-as many individual companies have-more than a million dollars this year, the government actually loses 52 per cent of the amount in taxes. I do not have any trouble in pointing that fact out to my friend the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann). For a small sum of money this

government could have put stability into that market and could have prevented the distress selling which actually occurred and which created these losses as a result of which I say the treasury here lost a great deal of revenue. I think we could have been wiser in the way we handled that matter last year. With the representations that my good friend the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair) will be able to make to the cabinet in the future, I hope such things will not happen again.
The fishing industry does not want to be spoon-fed. Those engaged in that industry are extremely independent and highly capable. But I should like to see the same consideration given to them that is given to the agricultural industry. In British Columbia we had a surplus of 500,000 cases of fish- I refer to canned salmon, the best in the world-and it is lying there as a threat to the market. In the agricultural industry, however, the Canadian government have stepped in and I believe they are now the proud possessors and owners of about 40 million pounds of butter in this country. Just the other day I read in the paper-whether I have inferred too much from what I saw there I do not know-that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) suggested that this 40 million pounds of butter be kept from the market in order to stabilize the price of butter.

But at the same time I should like us to assist, if we can, the Minister of Fisheries in bringing before his colleagues the way the members from the fishery ridings feel with regard to matters of this kind.
There are many aspects of the fishing industry, and they cannot all be discussed in one short debate like this one. I apologize for having taken up this much time when I know there are many other hon. members who wish to speak. Now that we have this new Minister of Fisheries I am sure the
