subtopic: SUGGESTED INVESTIGATION OF ECONOMIC CONDITIONS IN FISHING INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to begin by complimenting the hon. member for Charlotte (Mr. Stuart) on bringing this resolution before the house. Since practically all my constituents are fishermen, I should be remiss in my duty if I did not rise in my place to support this resolution and endorse the constructive suggestions put forth by my colleagues.
I am sure my constituents would also wish me to take advantage of this opportunity to express to the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair), to his colleagues in the cabinet and to the officials of his department their sincere gratitude for what has already been done in their interest. Without the deficiency payments on shore-cured fish in 1951 and 1952 the families of many of our shore fishermen would have had to go without sufficient food, clothing and fuel, and the fishermen themselves would have been forced to leave the fishing industry altogether in order to seek more remunerative employment.
The bounty of $165 per ton for certain classes of fishing boats is enabling many fishermen to provide themselves with suitable vessels essential to the use of modern methods of fish production. The success of the experiments with the long-liners which were carried out by the federal government has caught the interest and the imagination of our Newfoundland fishermen, many of whom are now providing themselves with this type of boat.
The discovery of rich, new inshore fishing grounds by the fisheries research department has opened up easily accessible sources of supply hitherto unknown. This has been an added incentive to encourage fishermen to modernize their fishing methods. The research department is at present engaged in an experiment with the artificial drying of light salted fish. If a satisfactory solution to this problem can be found, and one that is economically feasible, it will be one of the greatest single contributions ever made to the welfare of our Newfoundland fishermen. Along with these there have been many lesser achievements such as the expansion of the patrol service and particularly the protection of the inland fisheries by increasing the staff of river guardians.
I think it is right to mention these things because human memory is short and we are prone to forget our benefits and remember only our needs. Though much has already been done, a great deal more remains to be
Fisheries
achieved. We need far more river guardians not only in my own riding but throughout the whole province of Newfoundland, particularly along the salmon rivers of Labrador. Our patrol service needs to be improved by the use of faster and more suitable vessels.
We also need to concentrate more on fishery research and conservation. We need to locate and learn about the movements of the large schools of herring which frequent the shores of our province and which we know to exist. The herring industry alone is capable of being developed so that its value will exceed that of all other fish caught in Newfoundland. We need more experiments with the curing of different varieties of fish, with the canning of fish and also with fancy cured fish. This will take considerable time and will require a great deal of money; but these projects are primarily a federal responsibility.
We need also more research with respect to salt-cured fish. What is a light salted fish? What is a heavy salted fish? Fishermen in various parts of Newfoundland have different answers to this question. The answer is all the more complicated because the salinity of the salt used is hardly ever uniform, even for the same grade of salt. Definite answers to these questions must be provided before standardization of quality can take place.
I am one of those who believe there will always be a market for salt-cured fish. People who live in hot climates lose a great deal of salt from their bodies due to excessive perspiration. This salt is essential to health and must be replaced. The cheapest source for replacement is salt-cured fish in which the salt is combined with high-grade protein which is also an essential to health.
Some economists advise us that the salt cod market is not economical and that we should get out of it as quickly as possible. The answer is that we cannot get out of it even if we want to; but I do not think we should want to because those people in hot countries need fish for food; and if they are poor people, they need cheap fish. I think we should put people's needs first. I believe that if we have the courage and the faith to put the motive of feeding hungry people ahead of the profit motive, then other factors will come into play which the economist does not ordinarily take into consideration and which will automatically provide the profits which the producers need.
I do hope also that some means will be found to provide unemployment insurance for our fishermen. A beginning in this direction could be made by making eligible those fishermen who are employed on monthly wages.

Fisheries
Above all, Mr. Speaker, we need a better deal for the primary producers. The farmers and the fishermen have very much in common; they are both primary producers. These primary producers are the people who run the risks, take all the hazards and endure all the hardships. Very often they risk their lives and everything they own. We want them to have as good a deal as possible. Scientific research can do much to minimize the hardship and reduce the risk, but before the fishermen can be in a position to take advantage of those benefits some capital assistance will be necessary.
The fishing industry is the second largest food producing industry in Canada, and though its market value is much smaller than the value of farm products, yet it is of sufficient importance to justify the consideration that has been requested for it today.
Again I should like to express my gratitude to the hon. member for Charlotte (Mr. Stuart) for providing this opportunity to debate this resolution and to focus upon the fishing industry the attention that its importance warrants.

subtopic: SUGGESTED INVESTIGATION OF ECONOMIC CONDITIONS IN FISHING INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with pleasure that I rise to support this motion by the hon. member for Charlotte, because the underlying ideas that are expressed in it have already been mentioned by me in this house on more than one occasion. I too am of the opinion that this government should pass legislation designed to render assistance to the fishing industry comparable to the legislation already enacted to provide assistance for agriculture. I too think it would be a good idea to establish a board to investigate the economic condition of the fishing industry of Canada with a view to making the necessary recommendations.
I am particularly interested in problems concerning fishermen because, as I discovered recently when looking up some figures, although my county is not by any means the largest in the province, it is the county in the province of Quebec which has the most fishermen. All problems that concern fishermen are therefore of vital importance to my constituents.
The fishing industry is also very important to Canada, as I had occasion to point out in a speech I made in the house on April 27, 1950, as reported at page 1940 of Hansard, as follows:
The fishing industry in our country has become very important indeed, particularly in view of the fact that we now have Newfoundland as our tenth province. At least seven provinces are vitally interested in the fishing industry. There are,

of course, Newfoundland, the three maritime provinces, Quebec, also Manitoba because of the extensive fishing industry in lake Winnipeg-
I was interested to hear some of the members from the west support this resolution this afternoon because of that. I continue: -and the province of British Columbia. When seven provinces in our country are vitally interested in the fishing industry, then I say the government ought to do as much for that industry, on a smaller scale of course, as it does for agriculture. The organizations having to do and dealing with fishing ought to have the same scope of action as those which deal with agriculture.
We find in the statutes of 1944-1945 the Agricultural Prices Support Act. In the same statutes we find the Fisheries Prices Support Act. These two statutes are practically identical.
But in 1947 the government decided they had not gone far enough so far as agriculture was concerned, and in that year they passed the Agricultural Products Act, the long title of which is "An act to provide for the sale and export of agricultural products". In my speech on April 27, 1950, I said with reference to the Agricultural Products Act:
This statute gives the minister, subject to regulations made by the governor in council, authority to-
(a)	sell or export agricultural products to the government of any country or any agency thereof pursuant to any agreement made by the government of Canada with the government of such country or with such agency and for those purposes may purchase agricultural products and make such arrangements for the purchase, sale or export of agricultural products as he considers necessary or desirable:
(b)	on behalf of the government of any country or any agency thereof purchase or negotiate contracts for the purchase of agricultural products;
Paragraph (c) does not apply. I continue:
(d) enter into contracts for the storing or processing of agricultural products.
Under that legislation some very good contracts have been made with other countries for the sale of agricultural products, but I believe we should have something similar for fisheries. If we had it I say it would help in finding markets for fishery products of the country, and I am sure it would help in overcoming the low prices that fishermen now get for their output.
As has been said already in this debate, Mr. Speaker, the fishermen are primary producers, and as such they should be placed on the same footing, I respectfully submit, as other primary producers.
Amongst the fishermen in my county, and not alone amongst the fishermen-I find in talking with hon. members who have fishermen in their counties and who represent fishing constituencies that the same feeling exists amongst them-there is the feeling

that our fishermen are not getting a fair deal. There is a feeling that they are not getting a fair share of social security. Everybody in this country, apart from the fishermen, seems to be getting a fair share of social security. The fishermen feel that they have been let down so far as that is concerned. For instance, they have no catch insurance. Catch insurance is something that would be parallel to the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. It should be possible to start up some kind of contributory insurance that would permit the fishermen to insure themselves against a bad catch in any year in the same way that the prairie farmers can insure themselves against a bad crop.
It is very difficult for fishermen to get equipment insurance; they can hardly get it at all. I have made a suggestion to the Department of Fisheries, and I think it is a good one. There is a fishermen's bounty that is given to the fishermen every year under an old treaty with the United States, under which they get a bounty of about $9 a year. That $9 a year is of no practical use, but it could be used, along with a government contribution, as a contribution towards fishermen's equipment insurance.
We have a prices support board. When I came into the house as a new member, representing a fishermen's constituency, I had great faith in the Fisheries Prices Support Act and in the board. I thought now we have something that will help me overcome the problem that the fishermen are always complaining about, namely that the prices are not high enough. I pleaded with the board several times. I had special hearings of the board. I went before them and pleaded the case as well as I could, but I never succeeded in getting anything tangible from the fisheries prices support board. In 1951 I held out some hopes to the fishermen of my constituency. I said to them in a debate on the 24th of April, 1951, as reported at page 2363 of Hansard:
According to the information I have, the fisheries prices support board has not yet exercised its powers to set floor prices for fish and to make payments to fishermen. X respectfully suggest to the minister that the time has come for the board to exercise those powers.
I hope, therefore, Mr. Speaker, that the survey which is now being made in Newfoundland by this government will warrant setting a floor price for fish and that the first request of the fishermen will be granted.
That was never implemented. There was never a floor price set for fish, and the fishermen of the Magdalen Islands are still waiting for some help from the fisheries prices support board. Here is something the fisheries prices support board could do right away. Even if they cannot set a minimum 68108-91
Fisheries
price for all fish, the price of cod should be set because cod is the biggest catch in the Magdalen islands, and the price has always been low. It would take someone more versed in economics than I am to explain why, when prices have been going up, when the cost of living has been going up, and meat and vegetable prices have been increasing, fish prices have been going down or have remained stationary. The problem of the fishermen in my county is the price of cod.
Most of the cod produced is not sold fresh; it is sold smoked or salted. If the fisheries prices support board cannot support the price of all cod, let them at least support the price of smoked and salt cod, which are exported to countries in which the people are not very well off, and who are able to pay only low prices. This would be an opportunity for the support board to step in and do something about this problem.
Then with regard to unemployment insurance. The fishermen feel that they have not been getting their share of social security. One of our forms of social security in this country is unemployment insurance. Away back in 1951 I held out the hope to the people in my county that they might get unemployment insurance. At that time I said this:
As early as last spring, one year ago, I made representations to the unemployment insurance commission and the Department of Labour in order to bring fishermen under the act. The unemployment insurance commission began a nation-wide survey to secure the necessary information and data before reporting on this request. I understand that the report is in preparation and hope that the government will be able to include fishermen in the benefits of this legislation which has already been extended to lumberjacks.
I mentioned lumberjacks particularly, because they are seasonal workmen. That was in 1951. A report has been made, and it was negative. Nothing has been done about it. The report stated that in the United States and England they have unemployment insurance for fishermen, but they pointed out something about administrative difficulties which would have to be overcome.
I say that administrative difficulties are not a sufficient reason for not extending that form of social security to fishermen in this country. I am sure that if the Department of Fisheries will put its shoulder to the wheel, if members of the staff in that department will put their heads together, they will be able to find a way to overcome these administrative difficulties that have been overcome in other countries.

Fisheries
I insist again, as I feel it my duty to do, that the Unemployment Insurance Act should be extended to fishermen. And I say again that perhaps the first step would be to extend it to fishermen who are on wages or salary, fishermen's helpers particularly. There is no reason why they should not benefit from unemployment insurance, inasmuch as they are employees receiving wages, just the same as do other employees in Canada who earn wages.
One thing that would help the Magdalen islands particularly would be the export of fresh fish. To export fresh fish refrigeration ships, or a refrigeration ship, would be required. It would not be fair to put the whole burden on the federal government, because in my province the administration of the fisheries has been taken over by the provincial government. I make an appeal today to that provincial government, to the premier and to the minister of fisheries, and ask them not to forget the fishermen of the Magdalen islands. I would ask them to see that the necessary moneys are appropriated to supply refrigerators and the refrigerated ships required in the export of fresh cod. If this were done it would solve our problem to a great extent.
I call upon the government to give a new deal to the fishermen, particularly those on the east coast. I understand those on the west coast have their very valuable salmon crop, and I do not think there is any problem so far as they are concerned. Their economic conditions are good, when compared with the less favourable conditions of the fishermen on the east coast.
Let it not be suggested that fishermen are a forgotten race or a forgotten group of people. Let us see that they get what they are entitled to, the same as the other inhabitants of this great country of ours. They are a hardy race. They go out every day, courageously, wresting their living from the sea. They risk their lives to earn a living for their families and to supply food to the people of Canada. I say we should show some regard for these people, that we should show them at least the same regard we extend to the agricultural producers. I call upon the government to do its best for the fishermen of the Magdalen islands in particular, and of Canada at large.

speakeroldname: Mr. W. J. Browne (St. John's West):
subtopic: SUGGESTED INVESTIGATION OF ECONOMIC CONDITIONS IN FISHING INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member who introduced the resolution this afternoon made reference to a reply he received last year in a similar debate. It was pointed out to him by some speaker on behalf of the government that the annual value of agriculture was very much greater than the value of the fisheries.

I do not think anyone can deny that agriculture is a most important industry in Canada, because it is so varied and so extensive in its operations. It has increased in importance in the last few years. There can be no doubt that it is of tremendous value to Canada.
It would be very difficult, therefore, to make an exact comparison. But that is what is being done when we compare the amount of money that is being voted by parliament to assist agriculture, and the amount being voted to assist the fisheries. It has been shown that last year $11 million was voted for the fisheries and $74 million for agriculture. It was pointed out that agricultural production was ten times as great, and that therefore the fisheries are receiving all they should receive.
It seems to me it is not desirable to have comparisons of that kind in our arguments. Are the fisheries getting the attention they need? That is the point we must consider. Everyone has paid tribute to the brave and hardy fisherman who risks his life and faces such hardship on the rolling deep. Anyone who has seen a fisherman come in from the banks in the wintertime, on a vessel caked with ice, must know the hardships that fishermen must endure. Anyone who has seen the small man in his dory, rocking in the cradle of the deep, must know something of the danger that the fisherman goes through.
Anyone who has seen, as I have, men from different parts of Newfoundland rallying in great numbers, as they did in 1939 and 1940, to enlist in the Canadian navy and in the British navy to defend the shores of this country, must realize that those men are deserving of the greatest consideration, because if we did not have the fisheries we would not have suitable men to man the ships of the navy.
I know that help has been given to the fisheries beyond that set out in the estimates for the department. The large amounts that are voted annually for the construction of wharves and breakwaters are in the interests of fishermen, and those expenditures are appreciated very much indeed.
Well then, is there any need to help the fishermen, more than is being done at the present time? I submit that there is. I have been in settlements occupied almost exclusively by fishermen, and I have seen the poor circumstances under which they live. It may be that fisheries cannot be carried on economically in those places. But whatever the circumstances are, the conditions one sees there show that these people are not receiving the attention they deserve. At

the present time in Newfoundland a joint committee has been appointed by the federal and provincial governments to investigate the fisheries of that province. So I suppose the resolution is really answered, so far as Newfoundland is concerned.
Therefore I can speak only in a general way in the debate this afternoon. I feel Newfoundland has a special problem because only a few years ago the fisheries of that province were such an important factor in its economic life. Those fisheries have declined tremendously. We look forward with great interest and hope to a solution by this joint committee. A royal commission which investigated conditions in Newfoundland in 1932 found that there were 65,000 fishermen, while last year it was shown that there were only about 22,000. This is a decline of two-thirds in the number of people prosecuting the fisheries. There must be some reason why such large numbers are leaving this industry. They have left to go to work in Greenland, at Goose Bay, and at Seven Islands, the gateway to the mines on the Labrador-Quebec boundary. There was a bad year in 1949; another bad year in 1950; a not too good year in 1951. What is the use of men staying in the fisheries?
The new Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair) is young, he is aggressive, and I am sure he is interested. Let us hope we are going to get some help that will put the fisheries back into the place they should be occupying in the economic life of the country. Other speakers have referred to unemployment insurance, which is most important, and to the fisheries prices support board.
The question is at what stage the powers of this board should be invoked. Should we wait until there is a calamity? In 1951 I contended that the powers of this board should have been invoked, but that was not done by the government. There has been an interesting development in connection with the fisheries in Newfoundland. The fishermen have formed themselves into a federation with provincial government assistance. I recommended in this house that the federal government should give assistance for this federation, but that was not done. This federation of fishermen has been making fair progress, but I do not know just how far an organization of that kind can go in a short time. It needs a great deal of wise direction and guidance. I do not know whether ultimately it is going to be a success but it certainly deserves to be.
I come now to the important question of marketing. The principal agricultural product produced on the prairies, wheat, is marketed through a board. It does not

appear in the estimates, but the assistance given the farmers in the marketing of this product is tremendous. None of them would want to go back to the system which was in existence before. We have an organization in Newfoundland known as the Associated Fish Exporters Limited which has to do with the marketing of fish. The federation of fishermen have recently been invited to become a member of that body. I do not know whether that is the solution.
I think it was the mover of the resolution who drew attention this afternoon to the small amount of money the primary producer received for his product as compared to the amount the consumer had to pay. Along the way between the producer and the consumer are several middlemen, and a considerable sum is absorbed in profits, commissions, transportation charges and so forth. Those charges may be well justified, but the fact is that there seems to be a large gap. There is no reason why that gap should be so great; there is no reason why the fisherman should not get a larger share of the ultimate price paid for his product by the consumer.
It must be realized that the decline in the number of men engaged in the fisheries in Newfoundland is a serious matter, because we have always looked upon the fisheries as our most important industry. Despite the value of the pulp and paper industry, despite the value of the mineral industry, the fishing industry because of its extensive nature, because it is carried on by people living in 1,300 settlements around the island, because it spreads prosperity over the whole island to a greater degree than any other industry, is considered to be the most valuable.
I do not want to take up too much time this afternoon because I know several other hon. members wish to speak, and the minister wifi wish to reply. I should like to conclude by quoting the words of Oliver Goldsmith:
But a bold peasantry, their country's pride,
When once destroy'd, can never be supplied!
That applies to the fishermen of Newfoundland.

like to accept the invitation extended by the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Robichaud), Mr. Speaker, to those members representing constituencies in which the fishing industry plays a prominent part to add their voice to the plea that he and the hon. member for Charlotte (Mr. Stuart) have made today for further aid to maintain the great fishing industry of our country. I would therefore like to add a few words to the many arguments which have already been advanced today, speaking from the point of view of a member representing a constituency on the Pacific coast in which quite a percentage of the population are employed in the important fishing industry.
In 1951 we had almost a record catch of salmon.	This salmon was taken to the
cannery, but unfortunately owing to the acute market crisis which arose a very large proportion of that 1951 catch was held over. When the fishing boats put out to sea in 1952 the storehouses and the canneries were already filled. This difficulty of marketing the canned salmon, which is the predominant branch of the fishing industry on the Pacific

coast, threatened the industry. The loss of the export market in the United Kingdom also affected the disposal of the carryover of canned salmon.
In addition to that we have been threatened with increasing competition from Japan. The Japanese tuna fleet has been putting into the Pacific ocean, and has been sending canned and frozen tuna to this continent. In fact the Japanese canned tuna or tuna caught by Japanese is also beginning to appear on the shelves of stores in British Columbia, and thus to threaten the domestic market for canned salmon.
We realize that the government, in order to help the hog industry in this country, took certain measures in connection with canned pork. Canned pork has been definitely in competition with canned salmon from the Pacific coast. The Japanese fleet has also been putting into the north Pacific ocean, and according to a dispatch from the United States embassy dated August 18, 1952, that Japanese salmon fleet had already caught over 2 million fish. This is the same species of salmon that is caught by our fishermen. It is for these reasons that the Pacific coast fisherman is facing difficult times.
There is the Fisheries Prices Support Act which was introduced in 1944. We are told in the report of the fisheries prices support board for this year of the various ways in which that Fisheries Prices Support Act could assist the fishermen. The program, as given at the end of the report, indicates that in two small instances, during the year under review, the Labrador salted codfish and the Newfoundland shore-caught salted codfish, some assistance has been given. The fishermen on the Pacific coast do feel that the time has now come when some practical means of assistance must be worked out in order to maintain the standards of living which those fishermen on the Pacific coast and elsewhere have a right to obtain.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to avail myself of this opportunity to add my voice in support of this admirable resolution which has been proposed by the hon. member for Charlotte (Mr. Stuart). I believe that fishermen throughout the length and breadth of Canada will realize that in the hon. member for Charlotte, since he brought this resolution forward last year and again this year, they have a spokesman of whom they can well be proud.
I should like also publicly to congratulate the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair) on his appointment to that important post. This is an extremely important position, and he faces heavy responsibilities. He has large numbers of fishermen throughout the length and breadth of Canada looking to him. We hope he will be able to satisfy their many wishes and desires. Living as we do in an economic world we realize that oftentimes we do not have as much reward as we think we are entitled to for our labours. But in the present Minister of Fisheries I feel we have a man of resolute action who will help to build, on .a sound and firm foundation, a structure for the benefit of the fishermen of Canada and of this important fishing industry to which this resolution refers.
I do not think any hon. member will question the need for federal aid to agriculture, to a lesser or a larger degree depending upon the state of the industry and its ability to return to the primary producer an adequate return for his labours. As to the fisheries and other fields of industry, assistance should also be forthcoming when it is required. As to agriculture, we find that aids have been given and floor prices have been granted in many cases for commodities which are produced by our farmers. We are all in accord with and sympathetic toward help which has been given in that way. When $65 million were voted by this house to help the farmers, we felt that it was a good move. On the other hand, when the fishermen need assistance we who represent fishing constituencies are not remiss in our duty in rising to press their urgent claims.
Coming as I do from Newfoundland, which is now the tenth province of Canada, may I say we realize that in Newfoundland we have a tremendous source of food production. God in his bountiful beneficence has blessed our shores on the Atlantic ocean with countless numbers of fish of various kinds, and other foods such as birds. Of course the birds feed upon the fish, but they are a source of food for our people. As we think of the top soil of the world being gradually used up in order to supply the
needs of the growing population, we realize what a tremendous reservoir of wealth is contained in the sea. We also realize the need for conservation in order that these God-given blessings will be used to the greatest benefit, and also for the needs of the people from time to time.
As to Newfoundland, I am afraid that the benefits accruing to agriculture are something from which we are unable to profit to any very great extent. But we can and do supply our share of fish, minerals, pulp and paper and other products, which are today taking, to a considerable extent, the paramount place which in the past was occupied by the fisheries in the province of Newfoundland.
Assistance to the fishermen can be given by the Department of Fisheries in a good many ways. These have already been enumerated this afternoon by various members who have spoken, and I do not want to repeat what has been said. Hon. members have pointed out how the department has helped in the past in Newfoundland, and what assistance the department has given.
We have these bountiful banks but we notice that, coming from the other side, the trawlers from France, Spain and Portugal are fishing these banks and taking back for their people this important food. Fish which we had often in the past supplied to such important customers as Portugal, Spain and Italy is to a great extent being produced by their own people at the present time. While we cannot blame them for that fact, we realize the great distress this has caused among people who have taken up the way of life of fishermen and who now have to lay down their nets and go off in search of work as carpenters or in other avenues of employment. These people who come over from the other side and fish on our banks are sometimes encroaching, we think, upon the territory which should be reserved for our fishermen. There may be a need for the department concerned to investigate and to decide whether or not the territorial limits of Canada should not be extended coastwise.
As I represent the important riding of Labrador, I should like to say that down there we have a tremendous coast line. Unfortunately, since confederation the Labrador fishery has declined to a greater degree than previously, although that decline was apparent before we entered into confederation.
As to the long-liners with which experiments are now being made, I hope some day they will become high-liners, because the investigation carried out by the Department

Fisheries
of Fisheries has been the means of exploring further fishing grounds and of opening up other banks to which fishermen can proceed and catch a larger type of codfish; and it seems to me it is the larger fish that is in demand. We can readily understand that.
Unfortunately, on the whole, on Labrador the run of fish is of small size. It was my pleasure this year to catch some myself when I was down there. In fact, one morning before breakfast I got up and threw a jigger overboard; after a few jigs I pulled in a codfish. One of the United States tourists who was also on this ship was fortunate enough to get a codfish weighing 31 pounds. He has its head mounted. That shows what the United States tourist thinks of this fish. There is no lack of fish on the Labrador. These fish come in. It is only a matter of getting traps and fishermen and being able to take them. They come in in search of food. This year and the year before the fishery in Newfoundland was fairly good, brought about I believe to quite an extent by the inshore winds which prevailed before the fish left their feeding grounds and came to the shore. When you take into account the winds, the tides, the storms and the other hazards which the fishermen have to face, it is a calling beset, as has already been said, by great danger and also by much hard work.
I had prepared quite a speech on this resolution but I see that time is going on, and no doubt the minister wants to make a few remarks. I shall take the opportunity on another occasion to resume my remarks, but in the meantime I should like to say that since the minister is going to Newfoundland in a few days to address the board of trade down there, I wish him bon voyage. I believe he will hear from the people of Newfoundland, and since he will be there he will be able to see things firsthand and get their reaction.
The hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Browne) has already mentioned the Walsh report. We are all looking forward to it. It will soon be put into the hands of the government. As has been said before, the fisherman is an independent type of man. Sometimes when he is just moving along in his boat he is not looking to be rescued, but he is not moving at great speed. Then some of his friends come along and they think he should be moving a little faster, and because they have a more powerful boat they take him in tow. I think the fishing industry needs to be taken in tow by the federal government and given the assistance that it requires by research, by science and in every other possible way so that as a result the efforts of the fishermen may be brought to

fruition and their produce accrue to the greatest benefit of the Canadian nation.
